albums.blurb: David Axelrod was a staff producer at Capitol Records — behind Lou Rawls's mid-sixties hits and Cannonball Adderley's "Mercy, Mercy, Mercy!" — before stepping out under his own name with this debut, a seven-part instrumental suite inspired by William Blake's 1789 poetry collection. Recorded with Wrecking Crew session players including bassist Carol Kaye and drummer Earl Palmer, it fuses heavy breakbeat drums, baroque strings and psychedelic guitar into something between jazz fusion and orchestral pop, and its tracks — "Holy Thursday" above all — became bedrock sampling material for DJ Shadow, UNKLE and Swizz Beatz.
albums.reception: The album sold only about 75,000 copies in its first year and drew mixed contemporary reviews, but critics reassessed it as a classic in the 1990s and Pitchfork ranked it No. 144 on its 2017 list of the 200 best albums of the 1960s.

albums.blurb: Leslie Feist made her name in Toronto's Broken Social Scene collective before breaking out solo with Let It Die; The Reminder is its follow-up, recorded largely live with her band in a manor house outside Paris. It balances hushed ballads against buoyant, handclap-driven pop — "I Feel It All" and "My Moon My Man" among them — and its single "1234" became ubiquitous after soundtracking Apple's iPod nano commercial that fall.
albums.reception: The Reminder won Album of the Year and Pop Album of the Year at the 2008 Juno Awards and brought Feist four nominations at the 2008 Grammys, including Best Pop Vocal Album.

albums.blurb: Portishead formed in Bristol around vocalist Beth Gibbons, producer Geoff Barrow and guitarist Adrian Utley, and Dummy is their debut — alongside Massive Attack's Blue Lines, the record that defined the Bristol trip-hop sound. Built from slowed hip-hop breaks, vinyl crackle, spy-film guitar and samples of Lalo Schifrin and Isaac Hayes, it sets Gibbons's spectral torch singing in noir atmosphere; the band has released only two further studio albums in the three decades since.
albums.reception: Dummy won the 1995 Mercury Music Prize, the UK's album-of-the-year award, on the strength of its debut-year acclaim.
